title: While We Were Still Weak
speaker: Jonathan Baird
summary: God is the great surpriser. Christ didn't die for high performers. He died for the weak and the ungodly, and sought us out while we were sinners.
exhortation: A wonderful saint in our congregation said something recently that made my eyebrows go up: "God is the great surpriser." I wrote it down because it rings so true in my life, and this passage is a perfect example.

Our God is completely unlike any god in literature or any deity invented by another religion. We don't serve a God who demands our strength, insists that we get it right, or makes us put it all together before we approach him. We don't serve a God who demands constant sacrifice every time we come into his presence. Not anymore. Our God came to us while we were still weak. Christ died for the ungodly.

In human terms this doesn't make sense. As the passage says, one will scarcely die for a righteous person, though perhaps for a good person someone would dare to die. "But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Talk about the plot twist of all plot twists.

Christ didn't die for those who had proven themselves, the high performers, the best-looking or the ones who hit their numbers that year. Christ died for the ungodly and the weak. While we were still sinners, he came and sought us out. So this morning, are you surprised by his lavish grace toward you? Let's be surprised afresh by the wondrous, unexpected gift of God's salvation.
prayer: Lord, what should the posture of our hearts be in response to such grace? We have nothing to offer but our thankfulness and praise. Take all of us today and fill us. Use us for your purposes, so that your name is lifted high and glorified in all the world.

Teach us to walk in your ways today, so that in some way we honor and glorify you for the grace and love you've lavished on us: deeper than the sea, higher than the heavens, far beyond what we can imagine. Go with us today, so that your name is glorified.
